Obedience
o-be´di-ens
n. (hearing that does what is commanded; the Son's obedience unto death, and the believer's fruit of faith)
Latin obedientia, from obedire, to hearken, to submit to a hearing. Hebrew shama (H8085) is to hear, and so to obey. In Scripture a man has not heard if he has not done.

Biblical Definition

Obedience is not the same as being agreeable. It is doing what God has said because He has said it. Samuel put the knife to ritual religion: “Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams” (1Sa 15:22). The Son's own path is named with the same word: “he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross” (Php 2:8). Hebrews adds that “though he were a Son, yet learned he obedience by the things which he suffered” (Heb 5:8). That is active obedience as well as the suffering of death, and it is the righteousness imputed to those who are in Him. The believer's obedience is then a yielding: “to whom ye yield yourselves servants to obey, his servants ye are to whom ye obey; whether of sin unto death, or of obedience unto righteousness” (Rom 6:16). And it has a means: “Seeing ye have purified your souls in obeying the truth through the Spirit” (1Pe 1:22). Faith is not the opposite of obedience. It is the root. Obedience is the fruit. A faith that will not obey is not the faith of Abraham, and it is not the faith that justifies.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines obedience as compliance with a command, prohibition, or known law; and insists that voluntary obedience alone can be acceptable to God, and that obedience is not synonymous with obsequiousness.

expand to see more

OBE'DIENCE, n. [L. obedientia. See Obey.]

Compliance with a command, prohibition or known law and rule of duty prescribed; the performance of what is required or enjoined by authority, or the abstaining from what is prohibited, in compliance with the command or prohibition.

To constitute obedience the act or forbearance to act must be in submission to authority; the command must be known to the person, and his compliance must be in consequence of it, or it is not obedience.

Obedience is not synonymous with obsequiousness; the latter often implying meanness or servility, and obedience being merely a proper submission to authority.

Voluntary obedience alone can be acceptable to God.

Key Scripture

1Sa 15:22 — "And Samuel said, Hath the LORD as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the LORD? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams."

Php 2:8 — "And being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross."

Heb 5:8 — "Though he were a Son, yet learned he obedience by the things which he suffered;"

Rom 6:16 — "Know ye not, that to whom ye yield yourselves servants to obey, his servants ye are to whom ye obey; whether of sin unto death, or of obedience unto righteousness?"

1Pe 1:22 — "Seeing ye have purified your souls in obeying the truth through the Spirit unto unfeigned love of the brethren, see that ye love one another with a pure heart fervently:"

Modern Corruption

Obedience is treated as the enemy of grace, or as the whole of the gospel, and both errors refuse the Son's obedience in the sinner's place.

expand to see more

Cheap grace hears “not of works” and then treats obedience as a threat to assurance. Romans 6:16 will not permit a third category, a Christian who yields to no one. You are servant to whom you obey. If the truth has been obeyed through the Spirit, the soul is purified unto love of the brethren. A profession that will not hearken is the sacrifice Samuel rejected: religion offered instead of the thing commanded.

Legalism makes the opposite exchange. Obedience becomes the ground of acceptance, and Christ's “obedient unto death” is reduced to an example to copy rather than a righteousness to receive. The dictionary's standard is the active obedience of Christ imputed, as well as His death. Hebrews 5:8 is about the Son learning obedience in His humiliation, not about you climbing into His office. Your obedience is fruit. His is the title.

1 Samuel 15:22 also judges the evangelical instinct to substitute a better technique for the thing God actually said. Saul had reasons. He had cattle for sacrifice. He had a story. Samuel called it rebellion. Hearing that does not do is not hearing. That is as true of the regulative principle in worship as it is of the moral law in the life.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shama (H8085), to hear, obey; Greek hypakoē (G5218), obedience; hypēkoos (G5255), obedient; hypakouō (G5219), to hearken.

expand to see more

Hebrew shama (H8085) — to hear, so to obey; 1 Samuel 15:22, Deuteronomy 6:4, Exodus 19:5.

Greek hypakoē (G5218) — obedience; Romans 6:16, Hebrews 5:8, 1 Peter 1:2.

Greek hypēkoos (G5255) — obedient; Philippians 2:8, obedient unto death.

Usage

"“To obey is better than sacrifice” — said to a king who had a religious reason."

"“Obedient unto death, even the death of the cross” — the title, not merely the example."

"“His servants ye are to whom ye obey” — there is no third master."
